idiom_name: named event object + raise-at-transition + typed subscriber dispatch
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one immutable type per occurrence, named in the past tense, carrying the identifiers subscribers need plus an occurred-on timestamp; let the aggregate that owns the state change construct the event at the exact point of the transition and collect it until the unit of work reaches a single dispatch point. Provide a small dispatcher mapping event type to handlers, keep it behind a port so handlers are registered at startup and a recording double can replace it in tests, and decide explicitly whether dispatch happens before or after commit. Cross-process consumers get a separate integration event derived from the domain event - the in-process bus must not double as the messaging system.
code_sketch:
aggregate.confirm(order_id, actor):
    state = CONFIRMED
    events.append(OrderConfirmed(order_id, actor, occurred_on=now))   # raised, not dispatched

at the unit-of-work boundary:
for event in aggregate.pull_events():            # one explicit dispatch point
    for handler in registry.handlers_for(type(event)):
        handler.handle(event)                    # after commit; idempotent by contract
pitfalls: Dispatching inside the state change, before the transaction commits, either drags handler failures into the publisher's rollback or lets handlers read uncommitted state.
A registry keyed by event class silently ignores renames and subclasses unless registration is type-keyed by construction or checked for exhaustiveness at startup.
Event objects that carry references to live aggregate state let handlers mutate the aggregate after it has already been persisted.

Event loops (A→B→C→A cycles): when services mutually react to each other's events, infinite loops can form. Break cycles by introducing a dedicated workflow orchestrator or process manager at the coordination boundary.
Silent dead-letter failures: events that land in a dead-letter queue with no monitoring silently drop the failure, leaving the system in an inconsistent state undetected.
Cascading backpressure: a slow handler backs up the event queue, causing retries to compete with new messages, triggering exponential degradation across all handlers.

Out-of-order delivery on the same aggregate: two events for the same OrderId processed concurrently can apply in the wrong order (Cancel before Confirm). Use per-aggregate ordering (partitioning by aggregate ID) or sequence-number guards.

Clock skew on occurred-on timestamps: distributed systems with clock skew can produce events with timestamps that contradict causal ordering. Use logical clocks (sequence numbers, vector clocks) for ordering guarantees, not wall-clock timestamps alone.

Dual-write gap without an outbox: writing business data then publishing to a broker in a separate step creates a window where a crash silently drops the event. The outbox pattern (atomically writing the event row with the business data) closes this gap.

Treating domain events as integration events: publishing raw domain events to external consumers couples them to internal model changes. Always translate to a separate integration event with a stable, versioned schema at the bounded-context boundary.

Wrong move: treating the in-process event bus as decoupling -> consumers start inferring business meaning, ownership and timing from when events happen to be emitted, so the coupling reappears hidden in message semantics and handler assumptions and is harder to trace than a direct call -> instead treat each event as an explicitly designed fact-contract, and document the producer-to-consumer dependencies a producer accrues.

Wrong move: mirroring internal state (field-level updates, CDC-style row changes) as events -> consumers read the stream as a mirror of the internal schema and every refactor becomes a cross-team breaking change -> instead raise only business-significant occurrences and translate at the boundary into deliberately designed events.

Wrong move: using the event stream as the observability layer -> when a request fails you cannot reconstruct the causal chain from event payloads alone and wall-clock timestamps disagree across unsynchronised clocks -> instead wire events with correlation/causation IDs into distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry spans) and keep events for business metrics, not debugging.
